strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable question of interest to safe and robust RL researchers: whether caution in unfamiliar situations can emerge from learned reward uncertainty without explicitly designating safe actions.

The task sequence is informative, progressing from a universal help action to context-dependent caution and sequential driving. The distinction between single-image and all-images robustness also reveals useful differences in behavior.

The reported experiments show substantial behavioral effects: 1-of-20 selects help on 89% of single Fashion-MNIST images, and greater robustness reduces driving speed and collisions. The k=N controls help isolate the effect of risk aversion.

The performance-difference-lemma argument offers useful insight into extending CFR to discounted continuing MDPs with known transitions. The manuscript also explicitly acknowledges its tabular implementation and transition-certainty limitations.
weaknesses: Necessary for acceptance: reconcile the algorithm with its guarantees. Algorithms 1 and 2 accumulate max(0, immediate regret), whereas regret matching accumulates signed regrets and uses their positive parts to construct the policy. The printed update can incur linear regret; alternating two-action reward vectors (1,0) and (0,1/2) provide an example. Consequently, the stated no-regret guarantees do not justify this update. Identify which update generated the experiments and reconcile the pseudocode, implementation, and analysis.

Necessary theoretical corrections: Appendix C, Equations 11–13, reverses the required probability inequalities and omits the negative sign in the exponential. These appear repairable, but the displayed derivation is invalid. Furthermore, Theorem 3 guarantees performance for the best or uniformly sampled iterate, not convergence of the final iterate used experimentally. Narrow the convergence statement and distinguish empirical stabilization from the proven guarantee.

Necessary reporting corrections: Table 4 gives 99.08% correct actions and 1.80% help actions for the single-image 5-of-10 policy, exceeding 100% under the stated mutually exclusive definitions. Appendix B.1.2 reverses Figure 9’s interpretation of digit-like letters. B.1.3 claims accuracy improves with increased help reward, although Tables 2–4 show declining correct-action frequency for the most robust policy. These inconsistencies require reconciliation before the quantitative conclusions can be assessed confidently.

Necessary claim clarification: Section 3 states that computational cost does not scale with state-space size, contradicting the tabular policy evaluation described in Appendix B.2. It also describes finite k-of-N optimization as optimizing CVaR, although the manuscript elsewhere correctly describes an approximation relationship.

Optional improvements: independently retraining ensembles would assess variability beyond reshuffling the same trained models. Reporting distance traveled alongside collision statistics would clarify the utility cost of cautious driving. These would strengthen the proof of concept; larger benchmarks or state-of-the-art performance are not prerequisites for acceptance.
